title: hCG in Early Pregnancy: A Question, Not an Answer
summary: Follow serial hCG in a pregnancy of unknown location, see why the 48-hour rise threshold has changed, and why a “discriminatory zone” never diagnoses ectopic pregnancy on its own.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 26 Hit 1 (core: hCG discriminatory zone) and Hit 2 (hCG rise; progesterone) and the Figure 26 anchor. Checked against Farren 2026, Bobdiwala 2017, Pereira 2019 and Nwabuobi 2017. The reviewer’s fixed zone and 53% rule are corrected — register flags rv-hcg-zone and rv-hcg-rise. Pending: progesterone cut-offs in ng/mL (< 5, > 20).

objectives: Describe how hCG behaves in an early viable intrauterine pregnancy.
Define a pregnancy of unknown location and interpret serial 48-hour hCG changes.
Explain the limits of the discriminatory zone and of progesterone.

scenes.title: Positive test, bleeding — and an empty uterus on scan
scenes.altText: A patient with a positive pregnancy test and light bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows no pregnancy in the uterus and none elsewhere. Serum hCG is 2,500 mIU/mL. A tempting conclusion: “above the discriminatory zone, so it must be ectopic.”

cues.text: A woman has a positive pregnancy test and light bleeding.
The transvaginal scan shows no pregnancy — not in the uterus, not anywhere else. Her serum h-C-G is 2,500.
It’s tempting to call it ectopic straight away. Should the lab number make that decision?

scenes.title: Normal: hCG in a growing pregnancy
scenes.altText: hCG is made by trophoblast cells and keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone in early pregnancy. In an early viable intrauterine pregnancy, serum hCG rises roughly exponentially — doubling about every 1.5–2 days — until it plateaus later in the first trimester. A log-scale graph shows the rising line.

cues.text: h-C-G is made by the trophoblast — the cells that become the placenta. Early on, it keeps the corpus luteum producing progesterone.
In an early, viable pregnancy in the uterus, serum h-C-G climbs roughly exponentially, often doubling every day and a half to two days.
On a log scale, that looks like a straight rising line.
Serum h-C-G is measured quantitatively, so two values 48 hours apart can show how fast it is changing.

scenes.title: What changes: a pregnancy of unknown location
scenes.altText: PUL: a positive test with no pregnancy seen on transvaginal scan — a classification, not a diagnosis. Three possible outcomes appear: an early intrauterine pregnancy not yet visible, a failing pregnancy, or an ectopic pregnancy. Serial hCG lines: rising ≥ 35% in 48 h (consistent with a viable intrauterine pregnancy in a large study); a slow rise (seen in both ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage); a fall (failing pregnancy). Caveat: 10–20% of ectopic pregnancies show hCG changes that mimic a normal pregnancy.

cues.text: When the test is positive but the scan shows nothing, the label is pregnancy of unknown location. It’s a classification, not a diagnosis.
There are three possibilities: a normal pregnancy that is still too early to see, a pregnancy that is failing, or an ectopic pregnancy.

Serial h-C-G helps sort them. In a large study, viable intrauterine pregnancies rose at least 35 percent in 48 hours. A falling level suggests a failing pregnancy. A slow rise can mean ectopic — or miscarriage.
But no pattern is perfect. In ten to twenty percent of ectopic pregnancies, the h-C-G rise looks normal.

props.title: PUL: positive test, nothing seen on scan

props.label: 10–20% of ectopics mimic a normal rise

scenes.title: In the lab: the “discriminatory zone” is a guide, not a verdict
scenes.altText: Discriminatory zone card: the classic idea is an hCG level (often quoted 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL) above which an intrauterine sac should be visible on transvaginal scan. Cautions: the value varies between centres and ultrasound equipment (some protocols use 3,500); most ectopic pregnancies are visualised at hCG < 1,000; a single hCG above the zone with no sac must not be used to diagnose ectopic pregnancy or justify methotrexate, which could harm a viable pregnancy. Progesterone predicts viability, not location. Management uses serial hCG plus repeat ultrasound and clinical review.

cues.text: The discriminatory zone is the h-C-G level above which a pregnancy in the uterus should be visible on a vaginal scan. It’s often quoted as 1,500 to 2,000.
But it varies with centre and equipment — some protocols use 3,500 — and most ectopic pregnancies are actually seen at levels below 1,000.
So a single value above the zone, with no sac, must never be used alone to diagnose ectopic pregnancy or to give methotrexate. That could end a healthy pregnancy.
Progesterone helps judge whether a pregnancy is viable, but not where it is. The answer comes from serial h-C-G, repeat scans and the clinical picture together.

props.title: Serial hCG + repeat scan + clinical review

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “hCG above the zone with no sac = ectopic, give methotrexate” is crossed out → “Repeat hCG and scan; a viable IUP may still be too early.” Trap card: “A 48-h rise under 53% means abnormal” is crossed out → “Newer data: viable IUPs rise ≥ 35%; 53% misclassifies some.” Trap card: “A normal doubling rules out ectopic” is crossed out → “10–20% of ectopics mimic normal.”

cues.text: Trap one: an h-C-G above the zone with no sac on scan is not proof of ectopic pregnancy. Repeat the h-C-G and the scan before treating.
Trap two: older teaching said a rise under 53 percent is abnormal. Newer data put the minimum rise for a viable pregnancy at about 35 percent.
Trap three: a normal-looking rise doesn’t rule out ectopic. Some ectopics mimic it.

scenes.title: PUL is a question, not an answer
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “PUL is a question, not an answer — ask it twice (48 h) and look again (scan).” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: a pregnancy of unknown location is a question, not an answer. Ask it twice — 48 hours apart — and look again with the scan.
Where it breaks: thresholds depend on the starting level, the population and the assay; twins and heterotopic pregnancies don’t follow the rules; and protocols differ between hospitals.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “PUL: serial hCG (≥ 35% rise fits viable IUP) + repeat scan”, “The discriminatory zone guides scanning — it never diagnoses ectopic on its own”.

cues.text: In a pregnancy of unknown location, follow serial h-C-G and repeat the scan — a rise of at least 35 percent fits a viable pregnancy, and no single value above a discriminatory zone diagnoses ectopic pregnancy.

props.label: PUL → serial hCG (≥ 35% rise fits viable IUP) + repeat scan
Discriminatory zone guides — never diagnoses ectopic alone

explanation.what: Plain language: hCG is the pregnancy hormone; in a healthy early pregnancy it rises quickly, and a positive test with nothing visible on scan needs repeat testing rather than a snap diagnosis. Scientific terms: trophoblast-derived hCG supports the corpus luteum; a pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is a classification when a positive test is not matched by a visualised pregnancy on transvaginal ultrasound.
explanation.why: hCG production increases with trophoblast mass, so viable pregnancies show a characteristic minimum rise; failing pregnancies fall; ectopic pregnancies are variable and can mimic normal rises. Ultrasound visibility depends on equipment and operator, so any single hCG “discriminatory” level is approximate.
explanation.measure: Serial serum hCG 48 h apart: minimal rise for a viable IUP ≈ 35% (older 53% figure misclassifies some viable pregnancies); falling values suggest failure; 10–20% of ectopics mimic normal. Discriminatory zone classically ~1,500–2,000 mIU/mL (TVS), varies (some use 3,500); most ectopics are seen at hCG < 1,000; never diagnose ectopic or give methotrexate on a single value. Progesterone predicts viability, not location.
explanation.differs: Viable IUP (adequate rise, later visible sac) vs failing pregnancy (falling hCG) vs ectopic (variable); single hCG vs serial trend; classification (PUL) vs diagnosis.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: discriminatory-zone scenarios, interpreting a 48-hour hCG change, and what progesterone can and cannot tell you.

questions.stem: A patient has a positive pregnancy test, hCG 2,500 mIU/mL and no intrauterine or adnexal pregnancy on transvaginal scan. She is stable. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat serum hCG in 48 hours with follow-up ultrasound
options.rationale: Correct. This is a pregnancy of unknown location; a single value above a discriminatory zone does not diagnose ectopic pregnancy.
Incorrect. Treating on one value risks harming a viable intrauterine pregnancy.

options.text: Reassure that the pregnancy is normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Location and viability are unknown.
Incorrect. Quantitative serum hCG is needed for trends.

questions.stem: Serum hCG rises from 1,200 to 1,700 mIU/mL in 48 hours (about 42%). How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Consistent with a viable intrauterine pregnancy, though not diagnostic
options.rationale: Correct. Newer data put the minimal 48-h rise for a viable IUP at about 35%.

options.text: Definitely abnormal because it is below 53%
options.rationale: Incorrect. The older 53% threshold misclassifies some viable pregnancies.
Incorrect. A rise in this range fits a viable IUP; ectopics are variable.
Incorrect. Failing pregnancies usually show falling hCG.

questions.stem: What can a single serum progesterone value tell you in a pregnancy of unknown location?

options.text: Whether the pregnancy is likely viable, but not where it is
options.rationale: Correct. Progesterone predicts viability but not location.
Incorrect. Progesterone cannot locate the pregnancy.
Incorrect. Progesterone does not date a pregnancy.
Incorrect. It is a useful marker of viability.

references.usedFor: Discriminatory zone concept (TVS > 1,500 IU/l) historically assumed; PUL defined after a competent scan; slow hCG rise in both ectopic and miscarriage; 10–20% of ectopics mimic normal hCG changes; serial hCG cannot reliably discriminate location (meta-analysis); progesterone reflects hCG changes.

references.citation: Bobdiwala S, Al-Memar M, Farren J, Bourne T. Factors to consider in pregnancy of unknown location. Womens Health (Lond). 2017;13(2):27-33.
references.usedFor: PUL is a classification not a diagnosis; single hCG not helpful; discriminatory zone should not decide timing of TVS or diagnose EP; most EPs visualised at hCG < 1,000 IU/L; using the zone to justify methotrexate is dangerous; progesterone predicts viability not location.

references.citation: Pereira PP, Cabar FR, Gomez ÚT, Francisco RPV. Pregnancy of unknown location. Clinics (Sao Paulo). 2019;74:e1111.
references.usedFor: Discriminatory value varies across centres and equipment; protocol using 3,500 mIU/mL; 53% minimum rise (older study) vs 35% minimal 48-h rise in 1,249 PUL patients (99.9% CI).

references.citation: Nwabuobi C, Arlier S, Schatz F, et al. hCG: biological functions and clinical applications. Int J Mol Sci. 2017;18(10):2037.
references.usedFor: Trophoblast hCG maintains corpus luteum progesterone; doubling ~1.5–2 days in viable pregnancy; 53% vs 35% minimal rise; discriminatory zone 1,500–2,000 mIU/mL as classically used.

claims.text: Trophoblast hCG supports corpus luteum; doubles ~1.5–2 days in early viable IUP.
PUL is a classification; outcomes early IUP, failing pregnancy, ectopic; ≥ 35% 48-h rise fits viable IUP; 10–20% of ectopics mimic normal.
Discriminatory zone ~1,500–2,000 varies (some 3,500); most ectopics seen < 1,000; never diagnose ectopic or give methotrexate on one value.
Progesterone < 5 ng/mL = abnormal (100% specific); > 20 ng/mL usually normal IUP.
claims.note: Not taught; sources read use different (nmol/L) thresholds.
